newsitem.title: UK: EIU upgrades risk scores for 12 countries, 9 slip.
newsitem.headline: EIU upgrades risk scores for 12 countries, 9 slip.

text.p: The Economist Intelligence Unit's Country Risk Service has upgraded various risk ratings for 12 developing countries over the past quarter, while nine have been downgraded. Eastern Europe again comes out best.
The EIU upgraded its ratings for Croatia, Mecedonia, Russia, Slovenia, Ukraine and Yugoslavia (Serbia-Montenegro) but no country in the region suffered a risk deterioration.

In the former Yugoslavia, the report states "the change has in part been linked to the process of gradual political normalisation which has followed the signing of the Dayton peace accords at the end of 1995", the EIU report said. Russia and Ukraine showed a declining risk "score" but not enough to change their overall rating, while the former Soviet states progressed, but remained "by far the riskiest region in the world".

In sharp contrast, the report said, in the Middle East Israel and Yemen's credit risk increased. Israel was pushed from a "B" rating to a "C", the first change in three years, reflecting a "worsening political and policy risk".

"The election of Benjamin Netanyahu...brought with it a new and more unstable era in Israeli politics, and there is little doubt that his approach to the peace process will continue to anger the Arab states as a whole," the report said.

"Moreover, with the mechanics of the ruling Likud coalition likely to make effective government more difficult, notably in the area of fiscal policy, this will have an adverse impact on Israel's creditworthiness."

In the Asia-Pacific region, Bangladesh was upgraded on the back of improved political and policy risk after the general elections in June. But Indonesia, facing growing unease about the succession to President Suharto, now 75, and a "perceptible loss of policy coherence", was downgraded.
The country also faces a widening current account deficit and a growing external debt, the EIU said.
Winners in Latin America and the Caribbean were the Dominican Republic, El Salvador and Trinidad and Tobago, while losers were named as Honduras, Jamaica and Uruguay.
Uruguay's "greater dependence upon external dissaving tipped the gross national savings/investment ratio below 90 percent, triggering a deterioration in its medium term lending risk".

The Dominican Republic's short term trade risk was upgraded because payment delays have been shortened to two months (even though there is only two months worth of cover in foreign reserves) because of stronger foreign exchange earnings.

The report said Jamaica's political and policy risk score had improved but its "anti-inflation strategy remains risky since it relies also on a heavily overvalued exchange rate to depress import costs".
"We expect a significant deterioration in Jamaica's external position in 1996-7, triggering a 10-point increase in medium-term lending risk," the EIU added.
Honduras was "increasingly at odds with the IMF...in particular there is disagreement over the privatisation of public utilities and over foreign debt restructuring".
In Sub-Saharan Africa, Kenya was upgraded, Zambia was downgraded and Tanzania replaced Zaire, with its "disintegrating" economy, in the EIU's regional coverage.

Zambia's domestic political situation "took a sharp downturn during the quarter" resulting in its political and policy risk being downgraded. But medium term lending risk, despite some withdrawal of bilateral aid, has not been affected. "Its already onerous debt situation is largely unchanged," the report said,

Kenya's political outlook appeared stable "despite the liklihood of some slippage in macroeconomic discipline prior to next year's election", which should ensure an uninterrupted reform programme, the EIU said.
